{"id": "55:62/q03", "question": "How do the later gardens compare in rank and excellence with the first pair?", "turns_on": "The force of dūn, the sequence of promised gifts, and how the two sets of foliage, springs, fruit, furnishings, and materials compare.", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q03/p1", "position": "The later pair is lower in rank, beauty, merit, or degree.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd say lower rank or merit in numerous reports; Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jurayj, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Mūsā connect the ranking with the foremost versus people of the right. Ibn ʿAbbās also links the lower pair to hidden comfort in 32:17 (al-Naḥḥās). A prophetic report describes a golden pair and a silver pair, with vessels and contents of the respective metals; al-Ḥākim authenticated a Companion version of Abū Mūsā's statement (al-Ālūsī). Al-Kashshāf's comparisons, cited by al-Rāzī, concern foliage, fountains, fruit, and furnishings at 55:48, 50, 52, 54, 68, 76. Abū Ḥayyān reports arguments from flowing rather than gushing springs, more abundant fruit, brocade-lined couches rather than canopies, finer silk, and ruby-and-coral imagery. Ibn Kathīr says flowing is stronger than gushing (55:50, 66), and that the first pair's earlier mention and the verse's wording signal superiority. Elmalılı says the first pair's branching qualities are fuller and embody the highest iḥsān. Al-Samīn calls this the apparent interpretation; al-Biqāʿī adds a difference in place and standing; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes similar blessings despite lower grace and honor."}, {"id": "55:62/q03/p2", "position": "The later pair is superior to the first pair.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the first pair is gold and silver, the later pair ruby and emerald, and the latter is finer. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to favor the later pair because its springs gush and it is intensely green, against the earlier flowing springs and branches; another report says its descriptions are more laudatory and its gardens nearer beneficiaries. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report al-Zamakhsharī favoring this reading. Al-Rāzī challenges the lower-rank argument: successive divine gifts lead recipients to expect each to equal or surpass its predecessor. Elmalılı and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī report the more laudatory-descriptions claim."}, {"id": "55:62/q03/p3", "position": "The rank comparison is uncertain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the majority's lower-rank interpretation has nondecisive supporting arguments. Kur'an Yolu repeats that characterization and permits either lower rank or two more gardens. Al-Rāzī explicitly calls the lower-rank reasoning weak in light of expectations raised by successive gifts."}]}

{"id": "55:62/q05", "question": "Does the dual جَنَّتَانِ denote individual gardens or categories?", "turns_on": "Whether the dual counts separate gardens or garden categories.", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q05/p1", "position": "It denotes two further gardens, bringing the described total to four.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, and Asad describe an added pair. {"id": "55:62/q06", "question": "What are the first and later pairs called?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q06/p1", "position": "The first pair is Eden and Bliss; the later pair is Firdaws and the Garden of Refuge.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī transmit this from Muqātil; al-Māwardī adds that each pair includes many gardens. {"id": "55:62/q09", "question": "Why does the verse introduce a further pair of gardens?", "turns_on": "Whether the added pair marks reward, enjoyment of multiple nearby gardens, or a numerical allusion.", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q09/p1", "position": "It extends the promised reward with a like gift or increase.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares it with the promise of the best reward and an increase at 10:26."}, {"id": "55:62/q09/p2", "position": "Nearby further gardens give the blessed joyful movement and prevent boredom.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī places them near the palace so their occupants can move between gardens."}, {"id": "55:62/q09/p3", "position": "The four gardens allude to the four seasons.", "reasons": "Ibn Barrajān distributes them between two groups and interprets the gold-and-silver report accordingly."}]}
{"id": "55:62/q10", "question": "How do Paradise's ranks affect spouses and visits?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q10/p1", "position": "Paradise has multiple deed-based ranks; spouses may choose and higher inhabitants may visit lower ones.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh says God lets the higher-ranked spouse choose, but lets the lower-ranked spouse choose if that spouse is better. {"id": "55:62/q11", "question": "Where do people who leave Hell stand in relation to God's close servants?", "turns_on": "How reports apply the verse's lower gardens to those leaving Hell and whether they can join the closest believers.", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q11/p1", "position": "They do not live among God's close servants; Paradise and Hell have differing levels.", "reasons": "Imam al-Ṣādiq answers Ḥumrān's objection with 55:62 and 11:106, 108; al-ʿAlāʾ b. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds that the Imam mentioned an unexplained station between groups and says the Qāʾim will begin with scoffers as retribution."}, {"id": "55:62/q11/p2", "position": "People released from Hell should not be placed among God's close friends.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh rejects that placement: they were neither unbelievers, who cannot enter Paradise, nor believers, who would not enter Hell."}]}
{"id": "55:62/q12", "question": "What is the verse's inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q12/p1", "position": "It describes gardens of spirit and essence for the foremost and brought-near.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī links the garden of essence to unity of witnessing the essence, beyond witnessing in the station of spirit."}]}
{"id": "55:62/q13", "question": "How does this verse connect the sūrah's descriptions of Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:62/q13/p1", "position": "It opens a second description, distinguished from the earlier gardens for the brought-near.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the sūrah distinguishes the traits of Paradise for the muqarrabūn and aṣḥāb al-yamīn; its refrain signals further gardens and favors. {"id": "55:64/q01", "question": "What does mudhāmmatān mean as a description of the gardens?", "turns_on": "Whether 'green' is a simple gloss, a saturated green approaching black, literal blackness, or an account of the gardens' felt quality.", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q01/p1", "position": "The gardens are intensely deep green, darkening toward black through thick growth and plentiful moisture.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Muqātil, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū ʿUbayda, Abū Isḥāq, al-Kalbī, al-Zajjāj and others tie the dark cast to water, dense growth, freshness or blessing. Al-Layth says crops acquire idhāmm when luxuriance darkens them; al-Khalīl and others define dahma as blackness. Alūsī traces duhma to night blackness and dark horses; Elmalılı calls the form a feminine dual intensive participle. Al-Naḥḥās reports Abū Ḥātim's acceptance of both idham and idhāmm in ordinary speech. Ibn Qutayba and al-Wāḥidī cite Dhū al-Rumma's Abyssinian image; al-Wāḥidī also cites al-Quṭāmī's green night, Dhū al-Rumma's green shadow, a ḥawāʾ garden, the khadrāʾ idiom for blackness or abundance, and Abū ʿAlī's contrast of white barren years in Aws's verse. Al-Qurṭubī adds dark horses and camels, a still blacker jaww, Labīd's dark troops in armorlike covering, Iraq's Sawād, green night and the use of greenery for a multitude. Al-Rāzī says black is the terminal color, white accepts every color whereas black accepts none, kāfir applies to black, and the Prophet's saying about joining the great majority illustrates sawād as a large community; cultivated land is called black against white bare land. Ibn al-Zubayr invokes 87:5. Asad cites Tāj al-ʿArūs for abundant watering and Qurʾānic green as ever-fresh life (18:31, 76:21, 55:76). Ibn ʿĀshūr's color account and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī's tree luxuriance are reflected in their glosses."}, {"id": "55:64/q01/p2", "position": "They are green or verdant; some glosses intensify the green without specifying blackness.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported with the simple gloss; Ibn Kathīr records parallel reports from Abū Ayyūb, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abī Awfā, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAṭiyya, al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Rāfiʿ and Sufyān. Al-Durr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmit Abū Ayyūb's report that the Prophet answered 'green.' Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says two transmitted glosses support his prior account of two images, though their fit is unclear. Ibn Kathīr attributes freshness to luxuriant interwoven branches. Elmalılı likens the emphatic green to Turkish yemyeşil and gömgök."}, {"id": "55:64/q01/p3", "position": "They are black or very dark.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Mujāhid deriving the description from dahma, blackness, like a dark horse. Al-Qurṭubī also reports Mujāhid's black or very dark gloss. Al-Durr reports Mujāhid's black gloss and reports Mujāhid, ʿIkrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explaining the blackness by abundant moisture."}, {"id": "55:64/q01/p4", "position": "The two gardens are at the highest degree of joy, beauty and freshness.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī gives these qualities as the purport of the description."}]}
{"id": "55:64/q02", "question": "How is the dual description construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the dual is attached as an adjective to the earlier noun or read as a predicate with an implicit subject.", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q02/p1", "position": "It modifies the previously mentioned two gardens.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās explicitly identifies the two gardens as its antecedent; al-Ālūsī gives this construction before noting an alternative."}, {"id": "55:64/q02/p2", "position": "It predicates an omitted subject: 'they are intensely green.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this as an alternative; Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies the implicit subject and compares al-Fajr, which implies an oath verb, 'I swear by the dawn.'"}]}
{"id": "55:64/q03", "question": "Why is the description separated from the mention of the gardens?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q03/p1", "position": "The interruption makes denial of either the gardens or their attribute deserving of censure.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains the effect of the intervening wording this way."}]}
{"id": "55:64/q04", "question": "How do these gardens compare with the earlier pair?", "turns_on": "Whether deep green points to ground vegetation and lower rank, merely marks a different stated quality, or is prized enough to favor these gardens.", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q04/p1", "position": "The earlier pair rank higher, with more trees, shade, fruit or broader blessings; this pair's deep green suggests lower ground vegetation.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, reported by al-Rāzī, compares foliage (55:48), springs (55:50, 55:66), fruit (55:52, 55:68) and furnishings (55:54, 55:76). Ibn Kathīr says the first pair's flowing springs surpass the present pair's gushing springs. {"id": "55:64/q05", "question": "To whom do the two pairs of gardens belong?", "turns_on": "Whether the two pairs reward one group or distinguish two ranks of people.", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q05/p1", "position": "All four gardens belong to those who fear their Lord's station.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports Ibn ʿAbbās assigning all four to this group."}, {"id": "55:64/q05/p2", "position": "The first pair is for the forerunners and this later pair for their followers or the people of the right.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Ḥasan's distinction between forerunners and followers; Iṣlāḥī distinguishes the muqarrabīn from the aṣḥāb al-yamīn."}]}
{"id": "55:64/q06", "question": "What establishes this single word as an āya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q06/p1", "position": "Mudhāmmatān is a one-word verse, whose boundary is fixed by transmitted arrangement.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān cites Ibn al-Munīr and Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī for its unique one-word status. {"id": "55:64/q08", "question": "Is mudhāmmatān the shortest verse?", "turns_on": "The measure used for shortest: counted words, letters, or disjoint letters.", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q08/p1", "position": "It is the shortest by word count; Ṭā Hā is shortest by disjoint letters.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes the two measures."}, {"id": "55:64/q08/p2", "position": "Al-Ḍuḥā and then al-Fajr are shorter candidates; mudhāmmatān and thumma naẓara are rejected under letter or word counts.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān gives the debt verse as longest at 128 words and 540 letters and uses counts to assess the shortest candidates."}]}
{"id": "55:64/q09", "question": "What does this one-word verse imply for the scale of the Qurʾanic challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:64/q09/p1", "position": "The challenge is at surah length because an individual verse can be only one word.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī adds that even the short surahs al-Kawthar and al-Ikhlāṣ are inimitable, so Qurʾanic speech at that length is miraculous (108:1, 112:1)."}]}

{"id": "55:78/q02", "question": "What does ism, the Lord's name, signify?", "turns_on": "Whether ism denotes the uttered divine name, its bearer, an inserted idiom, or an attribute; the nominative reading is cited for more than one analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "55:78/q02/p1", "position": "God's actual name or names, especially al-Raḥmān.", "reasons": "Elmalılı allows any beautiful name but privileges al-Raḥmān, which opens the sūrah; Alusi and Tabatabai identify that opening name. Qurtubi also connects the ending to al-Raḥmān. Baydawi says the name applies to the essence; Razi distinguishes the name from its bearer. Tabrisi adds that His names are most beautiful and free of evil."}, {"id": "55:78/q02/p2", "position": "The name means the named Lord Himself.", "reasons": "Damghani, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan state this directly. Elmalılı reports that this is one way of construing the reading. Razi calls this common and compares the earlier 'face' and passages where tabāraka lacks 'name' (23:14; 67:1). Ibn Jawzi reports it; Abu Hayyan compares 55:27. Elmalılı says Ibn Amir's reading leads some to it."}, {"id": "55:78/q02/p4", "position": "Ism means a divine attribute, which identifies its bearer.", "reasons": "Baydawi proposes 'attribute' as an alternative; Alusi explains that an attribute marks the one bearing it."}, {"id": "55:78/q02/p5", "position": "It is the Supreme Name through which seekers ascend to attainment.", "reasons": "Qashani describes the seekers' ascent from beginning to end."}]}

{"id": "55:78/q05", "question": "What does al-jalāl mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is glossed generally as greatness or specified by punitive or inward implications.", "positions": [{"id": "55:78/q05/p1", "position": "Greatness, grandeur and majesty.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives greatness; Tabari, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur likewise gloss it as majesty or greatness. {"id": "55:78/q13", "question": "What does the verse's closing praise express?", "turns_on": "Whether the close is described generally as praise and thanks or specifically as the supreme delight of divine remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "55:78/q13/p1", "position": "It glorifies God, confirms His favors and calls for praise and thanks.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi say the close declares God worthy of glorification and exaltation; Ibn Ashur calls it praise. {"id": "55:78/q16", "question": "How does the ending connect al-Raḥmān to neighboring sūrahs?", "turns_on": "One connection is shared closing praise; another is al-Wāqiʿa's fuller account of the destinies implied here.", "positions": [{"id": "55:78/q16/p1", "position": "Al-Qamar and al-Raḥmān end by naming God; al-Wāqiʿa likewise ends in glorification.", "reasons": "Razi compares al-Qamar's 'Sovereign, Powerful' (54:55) and al-Wāqiʿa's glorification after spirit, fragrance and garden delight (56:89, 96). {"id": "55:78/q22", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the closing name and paired attributes?", "turns_on": "The inward readings track the seeker's ascent, the lover's perception, or the relation of divine independence to effusion.", "positions": [{"id": "55:78/q22/p1", "position": "Seekers rise through the Supreme Name until they attain it.", "reasons": "Qashani follows their ascent from beginning to end."}, {"id": "55:78/q22/p2", "position": "For lovers subsisting after annihilation, majesty and beauty appear together without veiling each other.", "reasons": "Qashani contrasts this with the earlier stage in which each veiled the other before realized divine existence and return to the attributes."}, {"id": "55:78/q22/p3", "position": "Majesty is independence from manifestations; generosity is effusion received according to capacity.", "reasons": "Alusi presents this esoteric account."}]}
